sentences.text: Estimates for the length of Hylaeosaurus vary significantly among researchers, ranging from 3 to 4 meters up to 6 meters, though a 2010 estimate by Gregory S. Paul suggests a length of 5 meters and a weight of 2 tonnes.
The animal is described as having rows of armor plating on its back and tail, a long head, and a beak for cropping low vegetation.
Kenneth Carpenter described the skull and lower jaw remains in 2001, noting that the animal possessed a triangular postorbital horn.

Maidment identified two unique traits: an unfused scapula and coracoid, and three long shoulder spines, with the front spine measuring 42.5 centimeters and a fourth spine located immediately behind the skull.
The skeleton was the most complete non-avian dinosaur known at the time of its discovery.
Hylaeosaurus was one of the first dinosaurs discovered, found on July 20, 1832, by Gideon Mantell in boulders freed by a gunpowder explosion at a quarry in Tilgate Forest.
Fossils were found in the Grinstead Clay.

In November 1832, Mantell decided to create the new generic name Hylaeosaurus, and on December 19, he chose the specific name armatus, meaning 'armed' or 'armoured', referring to the spikes and armor plates.
Gideon Mantell originally estimated that Hylaeosaurus was about 7.6 meters long.
Mantell originally modeled Hylaeosaurus after a modern lizard.
Only limited remains of Hylaeosaurus have been found, leaving much of its anatomy unknown.

Richard Owen based the classification of Dinosauria on Hylaeosaurus in 1842, and Coombs assigned the animal to the family Nodosauridae in 1978. The genus Hylaeosaurus was named by Mantell in 1833, and Hylaeosaurus armatus is currently the only valid species recognized in the genus. Hylaeosaurus was the first ankylosaurian discovered, but its taxonomic affinities remained uncertain for a long time, with its parental group being the family Nodosauridae.
In the 1990s, some researchers mistakenly classified polacanthines like Hylaeosaurus as basal ankylosaurids due to a belief they had small tail clubs.

In 1840, Owen hypothesized that the asymmetrical spikes were not on the back but were incorrectly assumed to be gastralia or belly-ribs. Mantell suggested that Hylaeosaurus either had a row of spines on its back forming a dermal fringe or possessed the same appendage on its tail. It is debated whether Polacanthus is the same species as Hylaeosaurus armatus, despite differences in their osteology. It is also debated whether Hylaeosaurus was a basal nodosaurid or a basal ankylosaurian.
